## **RENEWed Airports - Transforming Brownfield to Solar using Multi-task Deep Learning on Satellite Images**

Vishal Bhalla

vishal.bhalla@tum.de

**Abstract.** Airports can mitigate climate change by harnessing solar energy to become self-sustaining and carbon neutral. However, estimating the solar utility is challenging in its nonstop operations. RENEWed Airports is a work towards building a system that identifies potential photo-voltaic (PV) solar panel installation spaces within an existing airport - the total area, long-term power forecast, installation cost, % energy savings, greenhouse gas (GHG) offset along with the break-even time to recover high upfront costs, without the need of a physical survey. This study focuses on the underlying multi-task deep learning setup for data, modeling and evaluation plan of a Multi-Task Attention Network (MTAN) trained on satellite and irradiance images that semantically segments the area available for optimal panel setup and predicts the potential energy by regression. A user study is conducted to support the circular economy (CE) setting of levying a ticket surcharge for renewable setups at large-scale public facilities.

**Keywords:** deep learning · remote sensing · solar airports · sustainable development · climate change mitigation · circular economy

## **1 Introduction**

Rooftop solar installations on buildings in cities are a powerful renewable energy source that limits usage from traditional fossil fuel based electricity generation methods [65]. It serves as a short-term solution in acute power crisis [64] and acts as a hybrid energy system [3] that substantially reduces domestic electricity bills. A microgrid is also used to generate profit by sending excess power to the main grid via the net metering approach which turns a traditional power consumer into a producer simultaneously [53], proving to be an energy efficient and reliable value add for commercial buildings [63]. Moreover, rooftop solar power production is pertinent to climate change mitigation and becomes even more important as energy costs rise and urbanisation intensifies [81]. However, a low level of energy literacy [5], income strata and rental structure of homes [33], high upfront investment costs [34] and long-term returns act as a barrier for its widespread adoption [45].

Moving to public utilities, an airport has a largely flat land with some low-rise constructions; rooftops of freight, terminals, hangars, apron and parking setups along with the open space ground between taxiway and runways in its infrastructure [1] present an untapped potential to harness solar energy. A brownfield airport remodels or improves upon existing facilities and constitutes almost all of the 17,678 commercially operating airports in the world [2], at present. Airports operate day-and-night throughout the year with a large volume of passenger and air traffic and, aviation activities directly and indirectly contribute in substantial environmental degradation [20]. Hence, [71,18] investigate airport buildings as potential large-scale solar PV power plants and [50] discuss streamlining and standardization of solar airports, while [38] analyze the performance of sustainable airports which have minimal impact on the environment.

The RENEWed Airports system leverages satellite imagery and Machine Learning (ML) approaches for planning solar setups at airports and potentially eliminates physical surveys to saves resources. This is helpful given the roundthe-clock operational nature of an airport, with potential security concerns and the risk to be near the runways. It intends to reduce current-system impacts with low-carbon electricity [55], cut down on GHG emissions, encourage peer adoption of carbon neutral airports [9] and, aligns to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UN SDG)[1] of _’Sustainable cities and communities’_ . A CEfriendly system reduces aviation costs for a sector that is already reeling under the impact of COVID-19 and expects a traffic surge post the pandemic [32]. The visible panels show a commitment to environmental stewardship, instilling a feel good factor amongst the travelers [50]. Additionally, such a setup increases the sustainability ranking of the airport and safeguards against any potential carbon tax implications in the future.

## **2 Methodology**

The system workflow in Figure 1 comprises of an offline setup at the top which fetches temporal satellite image snapshots of airports that have already installed solar panels. The solar panel area is labeled on these images and passed along with corresponding time-distributed irradiance maps and its solar energy values to train a multi-task deep learning model (see 4.2 MTAN) which learns over the segmentation and regularisation outputs. The learned model is then deployed within the RENEWed Airports system below that is designed to work on other brownfield airports using an airport code search option. It retrieves snapshots of satellite and irradiance orthomaps for the searched airport and passes it to the MTAN model that primarily geo-tags potential spaces for solar panel installation on the airport map and estimates the power density from the energy it can produce. RENEWed Airports also calculates the actual square metric of panel area from the segmented image, along with the installation cost from solar utility providers to serve as a building energy identification software. ## **3 Related Work**

Many Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques are used in solar power forecasting [76,13,4] for probabilistic day-ahead [83], short-term [78] and long-term [22] predictions. A taxonomy of Deep Learning (DL) models applied to the electrical utility industry (EUI) [46] shows a shift towards long short-term memory (LSTM) networks [78,87] and transfer learning on convolutional neural networks (CNN) [83,36] to predict the PV power output using weather element data. In contrast, aerial techniques using Light Detection And Ranging (LiDAR) with multi-resolution processing demonstrate a valuable tool to estimate solar potential (SP) [70] and also basis an urban 3D model [52]. The closest work to incorporate satellite imagery for PV power forecasting is by [12] while [80] include a cloud amount forecasting network trained with satellite images.

[57,29,3] study the design for utilizing PV solar panels on unused rooftop of buildings while [42,24] identify existing solar panels using orthoimagery. [59] use satellite images whereas [60] use LiDAR and land use data (tax parcels) to estimate both residential rooftop and community SP. Remote sensing with aerial imagery at a large scale, [30,44,28] automatically map solar energy systems to create a database and [66] detect oil and gas infrastructure.

[21] is the only known work that utilizes ML techniques to estimate daily Global Solar Radiation (GSR) within an existing solar airport setup while [50,56,71,67] discuss energy harvesting from airports. But, none of the previous work attempts to identify both the placement of solar panels and its potential energy on a nonsolar brownfield airport that too from a ML perspective which is the focus of this study. This work attempts to jointly learn both these tasks with a multi-task DL model that is novel in the aviation setup, to the best of the author’s knowledge. ## **4 Technical System**

## **4.1 Data**

A curated list of solar airports [8] is extended using online sources[34] to include latest installations and covers 186 locations within 134 airports across 15 countries. It details the _System Size (MW)_ , _Ownership_ and installation _Date_ over the years 1998-2020 amounting to a sizeable 281.88 MW total capacity where maximum (32) solar setups were placed in the year 2012. The text in the 92 unique locations was manually mapped into 24 broad _Location Types_ for consistency across airport infrastructures with a _Others_ category for setups on unspecified or multiple locations. _Area codes (Zip/Pin)_ was also added as a column to aid the retrieval of corresponding irradiance maps and energy values for the region. The USA tops the list with 70 solar airports, the Cochin international airport (COK) is the most diverse with 8 different location types in its setup and also has the highest system size of 33.6 MW.

There are five type of ownership models - Airport (99, 68.3 MW), Third Party (70, 207.62 MW), Tenant (8, 5.29 MW), Utility (7, 14.82 MW) and National Guard (1, 1.45 MW) with the count of airports adopting the ownership and the total system size in brackets. In terms of system yield per location type over the years (fig. 2), grounds (79.2 MW) - those adjacent to the airport (80.5 MW), airfield (15.69 MW) and cargo area (14.4 MW) are the top contributors while rooftops (15.82 MW) of terminals (12.91 MW), parking (12.5 MW) and public transport area (7.09 MW) are the next best sources for power generation within an airport.

Solar panel areas are manually annotated in the temporal satellite image snapshots of these solar airports using the Labelme tool [75]. Simultaneous time distributed Global Horizontal Irradiance (GHI) maps [61] are coupled with the RGB channels of ortho images and the labeled areas along with the corresponding energy (kWh) point values constitutes the training data for our supervised learning model. GHI is the total irradiance from the sun on a horizontal surface of Earth [54] and is used as a feature to estimate SP [87]. Energy values are estimated against area codes in the PVWatts[5] solar energy calculator, instead of retrieving it from local utility providers. We model this as a long-term forecasting task by fixing 1 snapshot per month over a period of 5 years.

## **4.2 Model**

Multi-Task Learning (MTL) is a machine learning paradigm that leverages useful information contained in multiple related tasks to help improve the generalization performance of all the tasks [86]. [58] surveys MTL in a DL context which can improve accuracy over separately trained models and [35] state that cues

from one task, in our case segmentation, are used to regularize and improve the generalization of another domain - energy potential. By sharing informative visual features, this setup is efficient in terms of data, memory and inference. We employ MTAN [39], an end-to-end trainable model that can be easily implemented upon any feed-forward neural network. It automatically learns both task-shared and task-specific features and an inherent robustness to the choice of loss weighting.

The multi-task setting allows configuring for semantic segmentation which is an image-to-image dense pixel-level prediction as well as energy regression. Deep convolutional encoder-decoder architectures like ResNet [26], SegNet [7] and DeepLabV3 [17] that applies atrous convolution to extract dense features for semantic segmentation are considered. The MTAN-ResNet design that supports more complicated and modern multi-task network backbone is selected as it uses ImageNet pre-trained features to benefit from regularization induced by transfer learning [48] and which can be expedient on satellite image data [15]. It consists of a single shared network with 1 convolution layer and 4 task shared residual bottleneck layers and, 2 task-specific attention networks - each comprising of 4 task specific attention modules using a similar bottleneck design as the residual block. Each attention module applies a soft attention mask to a particular layer of the shared network, to learn task-specific features. The task-specific decoders use Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASSP) modules that resample a given feature layer at multiple rates prior to convolution.

The multi-task loss is comprised of two loss functions; a cross-entropy loss averaged over each mini-batch learns the pixel-wise class probabilities for Semantic Segmentation while the L1 norm comparing the predicted and ground-truth energy point values is used for Energy Regression. MTAN utilizes Dynamic Weight Averaging (DWA) to balance the pace at which tasks are learned and only requires access to the task-specific loss values, avoiding separate backward passes during training to obtain the gradients [74]. Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with 0.9 momentum and 0.1 initial learning rate with cosine annealing decay [41] are the selected training hyper-parameters.

## **4.3 Evaluation**

The multi-task model performance can be assessed using average relative task improvements [43] over separate models trained individually on each task as a benchmark. For individual task specific metrics, [85,77] present the full range of segmentation evaluation methodologies where supervised metrics for semantic segmentation include: Pixel Accuracy (PA), Mean Accuracy (MPA), Mean Intersection over Union (MIoU), and Frequency Weighted Intersection over Union (FWIoU) [23,40]. Unsupervised methods that objectively evaluate image segmentation can be considered in this setup given the limited amount of initial annotated data, aiding the evaluation of new test images from other airports. On the other hand, to evaluate the performance of the future energy output prediction - Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), and coefficient of determination (R2) can be employed as the evaluation indexes [87].

## **5 Discussion**

Open-source interfaces do not provide a high resolution (min. 30 cm) panchromatic satellite image that is needed for the panels to be visible for annotation and be represented over multiple pixels [14], while the irradiance maps are for a larger region (e.g. country) level. To automatically annotate the solar panel area on the image, pre-trained solar panel detection models were also tried but it did not accurately mark the segments. A sample annotation on a cross-section highres image with solar panels is shared along with the modeling code[6] as a proof of concept for this ongoing study. The author agrees that the data collection and annotation quality setup needs further refinement.

This system does not design the actual placement of panels for which proprietary tools can be used, and needs to mitigate risks [68] from any communication signal interference, airspace penetration, bird strike, glint and glare [50,69,67], high sounds, dust settling in, and occlusions from frequent airplane movements. Furthermore, in using airport orthoimagery and statistics, the privacy and security of its design and passenger data should not be compromised.

## **6 Economics**

A comprehensive review of prospects of solar PV systems [51] looks at feasibility study analysis, policies, barriers, and recommendations. Government incentives and rebates [27,10] help in transitioning to solar power and similar measures to those which assess policy proposal profitability on residential PV plans [62,19] need to be incorporated by authorities to drive solar adoption in airports.

A feasibility study [73] evaluates the financial outcomes of integrating renewable energy systems and [79] explores the techno-economic and environmental benefits for airport electrification. In the context of circular economy (CE), [49]

## **7 User Study**

An anonymous user survey was conducted to evaluate a traveler’s understanding of energy needs at airports and its results were then analyzed to validate the hypothesis of the economic model. A google form[7] with questions pertaining to 3 major sections of _Air Travel_ , _Environment_ and _Sustainability_ along with an optional _Traveler Details_ section was prepared and broadcasted in extended networks. The participants were informed to fill in the responses assuming preCOVID times (2019 and earlier). Overall, we received 60 responses (see summary graphs 3 for select few questions) from 11 countries across 3 continents with a healthy mix of gender and professional diversity ranging from students to sustainability experts and retired professionals.

The questions gauged the type ( _[∼]_ 56% respondents travel both domestic and internationally), frequency (with _[∼]_ 44% traveling 2-4 times a year) and major purpose of air travel ( _[∼]_ 48% for Personal and _[∼]_ 28% for Business) to awareness of energy needs ( _>_ 73% participants agree that a lot of electricity is needed) and environmental impacts at an airport ( _>_ 56% are aware). Moving to their interest in a sustainable energy setup at an airport, _[∼]_ 85% of respondents feel it is the moral responsibility of authorities to invest in sustainable energy and _∼_ 63% would like to see the sustainability ratings while _∼_ 70% will be delighted

to see a sustainable setup at an airport and _>_ 60% preferring to travel via it. In terms of willingness to pay a surcharge on tickets while using such a renewable energy system ( _>_ 84% users are open to pay a minimum of $1) that extends beyond aviation where _[∼]_ 62% are keen to also bear a 1-2% surcharge on other large-scale public sector services including railway stations ( _[∼]_ 81%), bus stations ( _[∼]_ 52%) and parks ( _[∼]_ 45%) as the top 3 amenities.

Deducing the small sample set of responses, the RENEWed system proposes a _t_ = $1 (basis _[∼]_ 84% respondents) per passenger green tax on each flight ticket to recover the installation costs. A very low _s_ is assumed to be available for solar produce while keeping the installation cost _I_ to maximum, with a medium daily passenger traffic _P_ to arrive at a higher bound for the days required to arrive at a break-even state _B_ . For example, assuming that only 15% of a 10000m[2] airport is feasible for solar produce wherein 1m[2] of panel costs $1000 for installation, with an average of 5000 daily passengers it would take _[∼]_ 300 days i.e. less than a year to break-even the costs. From a sustainability perspective, [37] evaluate the performance of 30 airports and a simulation design on the number of installations, the actual incurred costs and energy generated, along with the time taken to break-even are some metrics for evaluation of the overall setup.

## **8 Conclusion**

This study discusses the data and modeling of a multi-task deep learning approach as part of a renewable building energy software to setup large-scale PV solar power in brownfield airports for climate change mitigation. It uses satellite and irradiance images to semantically segment solar panel areas and predicts the potential energy by regression. Furthermore, basis an user study on travelers, an economically viable model is proposed to make the work on the overall RENEWed Airports system practically realizable and sustainable in a CE setup.

## **9 Future Work**

Experimenting with increased time-frequency snapshots augmented with statistical measures like averaging, irradiance maps apart from GHI i.e. diffuse horizontal irradiance (DHI), relative humidity (RH), air temperature (AT) and exploring advanced semantic segmentation architectures in CFNet [84], CCNet [31] and ASTMT [43] is a future direction of research. The economic analysis could also factor revenue generated by carbon credits [88]. Holistically, the RENEWed Airports system will serve as a pilot for authorities to engage in policy planning and design of solar PV infrastructure for brownfield and greenfield projects that extend beyond the aviation sector to other large-scale and high frequency public sector amenities like railway and bus stations, stadiums, parks, fuel filling stations, university campuses, shopping malls, etc.
